newsitem.title: USA: White House denies changing policy to suit Asians.
newsitem.headline: White House denies changing policy to suit Asians.

text.p: The White House on Thursday strongly denied that President Bill Clinton made an about-face last year on immigration policy after being pressured by Asian-American contributors to the Democratic Party.
"This really borders on being outrageous," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry.

The Boston Globe reported Thursday that Clinton made a last-minute policy reversal after the Democratic National Committee vice chairman, John Huang, waged an intensive effort to influence Clinton's immigration policy.

It said Huang, for example, sent Clinton a strongly worded memo that said campaign contributors who raised $1.1 million at a Feb. 19 dinner were alarmed about Clinton's position on a provision that could have blocked a million Asian siblings of U.S. citizens from immigrating to the United States.

The Globe said Clinton changed his view on immigration policy during negotiations with Congress last March in a way that addressed what Huang's memo to Clinton called the "top priority" of Asian-Americans -- allowing foreign-born brothers and sisters of naturalised American citizens to immigrate to the United States.
It said Clinton had previously opposed this "sibling preference" based on the recommendation of a commission he appointed.
McCurry said it was "crazy" to suggest a connection between Clinton's position on immigration and Asian-American campaign contributors. He said he did not believe Clinton ever saw Huang's memo.
"To suggest that this had something to do with something that John Huang was doing on outreach to the Asian community is laughable on its face," McCurry said.

Legislation to change U.S. immigration law eventually died in Congress. But the controversy over Democratic Party fund-raising tactics last year, particularly Huang's role in getting contributions from Asian-Americans, lives on.

A White House spokesman, Barry Toiv, said Clinton did not make a last-minute policy conversion, that he then and now wanted to suspend the so-called "sibling preference" and find a way to deal with the backlog of applicants.
"Our proposal was not to eliminate but to suspend new applications for people coming into the country on the basis that they had a sibling who was a citizen here," he said.
But the Globe quoted the immigration bill's two Republican sponsors as saying they believed Clinton's fund-raising prompted a policy reversal.
"I never in my 18 years in Congress saw an issue that shifted so fast and so hard," now-retired Sen. Alan Simpson of Wyoming told the Globe.
